extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of advertising history; historians of marketing and general readers interested in historical advertising/quackery
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and describe recurring tactics, promises, and presentation techniques used by 18th–19th century quacks and mountebanks in printed and public advertising (newspaper copy, handbills, street spectacle).

rubrics_metrics.name: Extravagant and universal cure claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Assertions of supremacy over all rivals and the ability to cure virtually any disease or malady (e.g., 'confirms his supremacy over every dentist in this kingdom', 'challenges all known and unknown diseases', 'Hydrophobia cured in thirty days').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page gives many examples of quacks making sweeping, absolute claims about cures and capabilities. These claims are used to impress and attract patients; they are an anti-pattern for honest medical advertising. Examples: Patence's claims of 'supremacy' and remedies for 'man, woman, and child'; Van Butchell's 'Hydrophobia cured in thirty days.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Detailed dated testimonials and case histories
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishing specific case reports with dates and particulars of cures as 'confirmation' (e.g., lists of dated entries: 'October 5. A Gentleman ... in five Days made a perfect Cure', 'October 16. A Lady ... cured without poulticing or cutting').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text highlights lengthy itemised testimonial entries used as evidence of efficacy. These serve to create an impression of track record and reliability. They are a common tactic in quack advertising to substitute anecdote for proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: No cure—no pay guarantees and explicit warranties
rubrics_metrics.description: Promissory phrases and refund/guarantee terms such as 'No Cure no Pay' and product warranties (e.g., 'teeth comprised of six different enamels, warranted never to turn black').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quacks used money-back or guarantee language to lower perceived risk for purchasers and to bolster credibility. Examples from the page include explicit 'No Cure no Pay' offers and 'warranted' product claims. Such clauses also appear alongside promises of secrecy and gratis advice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precise, conspicuous location/addressing and signage
rubrics_metrics.description: Giving extraordinarily exact address and signboard descriptions to distinguish one practitioner from rivals (e.g., long physical directions: 'In the Strand, over against the Maypole, ... at the Sign of the Golden Cross, between a Sword Guttlers and a Milliner's Shop ... the Sign of the Sugar Loaf and Barber's Pole').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter notes quacks frequently supplied highly detailed location information and memorable sign descriptions to make them easy to find and to differentiate their business in crowded urban environments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectacle, theater and public performance to attract customers
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of theatrical costume, pageantry, music, mounted carriages, props, demonstrations and public shows to draw crowds (e.g., Mangin's armour, plumed helmet, organ music; Katerfelto's black cats and electrical experiments; public exhibitions with admission prices).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public spectacle was an advertising tactic: dramatic presentation, visible accoutrements and staged demonstrations served both to attract and to persuade. The text gives multiple examples of mountebanks using pageantry as their principal marketing tool.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-demonstration and use of personal displays as proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Displaying personal examples or the practitioner's own body/family to prove product efficacy (e.g., Van Butchell showing his embalmed wife; Mrs Harden advertising a hair-dye 'to be seen on her own hair'; quacks inviting customers to 'see its effect on him').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quacks often used striking personal evidence—living or preserved—as persuasive demonstration. The book highlights this as a distinctive, attention-getting tactic which blurred demonstration and spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inflated or fabricated titles and credentials
rubrics_metrics.description: Assuming grandiose, ambiguous or fabricated professional titles to imply authority (examples: 'Surgeon by Birth', 'Licensed to deal in Perfumery, i.e. HUMAN BEINGS', 'grand-master of the Egyptian mason-lodge', 'the greatest philosopher since Sir Isaac Newton').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter records quacks inventing or exaggerating credentials and honors to confer legitimacy. Such titles were used as a rhetorical device to impress lay audiences despite lacking verifiable standing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of long-form, flamboyant newspaper copy and handbills
rubrics_metrics.description: Inserting lengthy, bombastic advertisements and handbills in daily papers with flowery, sometimes incoherent language and lists of cures, testimonials and commands (the text notes advertisements 'rather too lengthy for insertion' and reproduces extended copy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long-form copy enabled quacks to combine testimonials, guarantees, instructive directions, and theatrical language in one message. The book treats these as a hallmark of historic quack advertising style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pricing as signal: admission fees, variable fees and ostentatious charges
rubrics_metrics.description: Employing admission prices, steep or variable professional fees, and price-based exclusivity or credibility signals (e.g., Katerfelto's seat prices: 'front seats, three shillings; second seats, two shillings', Mangin's heavy guineas, 'one guinea each hair', or 'two per Cent, of Five Years Profit').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examples show pricing used both to monetize spectacles and to signal quality/exclusivity. The chapter includes explicit fee structures in advertisements and sales pitches, treating them as part of the advertising strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of novelty products, branding and specific product features
rubrics_metrics.description: Highlighting purportedly unique product features and branded items (e.g., 'teeth comprised of six different enamels', 'Graham and his Celestial Bed', 'blacklead pencils' promoted as 'by far the best').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quacks and charlatans packaged goods with distinctive attributes or a branded name to make them memorable and marketable; the text cites these product-detail claims as typical tactics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal to secrecy, privacy and discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: Offering 'profound Secrecy if required', private consultations, and wording that emphasizes discretion to attract patients concerned with reputation or shame.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promises of confidentiality appear in the reproduced adverts as a selling point for sensitive conditions; the book notes this as a tactical appeal to patients' desire for privacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on novelty superstitions and prophylactics as saleable claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Exploiting popular superstitions and folk beliefs (e.g., selling a 'CHILD'S CAUL' 'particularly recommended to persons going to the Continent... officers in his Majesty's navy ... being exposed to the dangers of the seas' and promising preserved life).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter documents the commercialisation of superstition—selling amulets and folk remedies—as a persistent advertising niche, using specific audience targeting in copy.
